extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism students, and journalists interested in how news is produced and how routine practices shape news content
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying criteria for how routine newsroom methods, beats, and source practices shape what becomes news and how stories are investigated and reported. Useful for students, researchers, or practitioners evaluating news bias and newsroom routines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routines of news gathering determine ideological character
rubrics_metrics.description: There is little argument that mass media news projects a particular point of view. Fishman’s research shows how the routine methods of gathering news, rather than any hidden manipulators, determine the ideological character of the product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess news not merely by reporters' or editors' conscious attitudes but by the routine, everyday methods used to gather news (schedules, beats, reliance on standard sources). Evaluate how those routines systematically bias coverage toward particular perspectives or the status quo.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Beat: routing reporters through governmental and corporate bureaucracies
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations cover the world mainly through 'beats,' which tend to route reporters exclusively through governmental agencies and corporate bureaucracies in their search for news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating coverage, identify the beats used and examine how they channel reporters to predictable official sources. Consider whether reliance on beats narrows the range of perspectives and favors organizations that produce steady, usable material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on bureaucratic accounts as 'cases'
rubrics_metrics.description: It is part of the function of such bureaucracies to transform complex happenings into procedurally defined 'cases.' Thus the information they produce for newsworkers represents their own bureaucratic reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically examine documents, press releases, police reports, court filings and other bureaucratic outputs as reconstructions shaped by institutional procedures. Recognize that these 'cases' may omit, simplify, or reframe complexities; evaluate stories for unexamined bureaucratic framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignoring occurrences outside bureaucratic phases ('nonevents')
rubrics_metrics.description: Occurrences which are not part of some bureaucratic phase are simply ignored. Nonevents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check what is excluded from coverage: events or processes that don't fit existing bureaucratic categories may be invisible. When judging news comprehensiveness, look for systematic omissions caused by dependence on bureaucratic event-frames.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase structures and their use in interpreting activities
rubrics_metrics.description: The Uses of Phase Structures; The Detection of Events; The Interpretation of Activities — reporters use phase structures to turn happenings into newsworthy activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how journalists map complex activities onto discrete phases (e.g., investigation → arrest → trial). Assess whether these phase frames distort continuity or causal complexity, and whether they privilege certain source narratives that fit the phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preconditions of exposure and the beat round
rubrics_metrics.description: Preconditions of Exposure to the Newsworld; The Beat Round; The Bureaucratic Foundations of News Exposure — routines and settings that make reporters aware of certain events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze the logistical and institutional preconditions (deadlines, beat schedules, access arrangements) that expose reporters to particular types of information. These practical constraints shape what reporters can cover and how deeply they can investigate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods for investigating and formulating stories: fact-by-triangulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact-by-Triangulation as a Framework for News Investigation and Story Formulation; The Perspectival Nature of Events: Fact-by-Triangulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating reporting quality, look for use of triangulation: corroborating claims across independent sources or perspectives. Also note limitations: triangulation itself is perspectival and may still reproduce institutional biases if all sources are institutionally linked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filling-in: dealing with irregularities and missing information
rubrics_metrics.description: Irregularities and Missing Information: Filling-in — reporters actively fill in missing details to construct coherent stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how journalists handle gaps: do they make reasonable inferences, state uncertainties, or present conjecture as fact? Consider whether 'filling-in' practices introduce bias or false certainty into reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for believing versus doubting bureaucratic accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Fact’ and Bureaucratic Accounts; Reasons for Believing Bureaucratic Accounts; Doubting Bureaucratic Accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the criteria reporters use to accept or challenge official accounts: institutional reputation, consistency, documentary evidence, or corroboration. Note the asymmetry Fishman highlights—bureaucratic accounts are often treated as 'hard fact' while others are labeled 'unconfirmed' unless time-consuming checks are made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newswork, ideology, and legitimation
rubrics_metrics.description: News, Ideology, and Legitimation; The Sources of News Ideology; The Politics of Newswork — routine news practices contribute to ideological legitimation of prevailing political structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge reporting not only by factual accuracy but by how routines and source choices legitimize power structures. Ask whether coverage reinforces dominant institutions and norms regardless of individual journalists' intentions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research methodology for studying newswork (observation roles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodology I: Observations as an Apprentice; Methodology II: Observations as a Researcher — approaches for observing newsroom behavior and production routines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For researchers evaluating news production, consider participant-observation approaches (apprentice) and detached observation (researcher). Use these methods to capture routine practices, beat interaction, and newsroom decision processes that shape coverage.
